passages.where: Elijah has just stood against the prophets of Baal, and now the queen has sworn to kill him. Exhausted, afraid and convinced he has failed, he goes alone into the wilderness and asks God to take his life. The Bible sets the prayer down plainly and does not scold him for it.

God's answer comes in a striking order. Before any words of correction, an angel touches Elijah and gives him bread and water, and he sleeps. Then a second meal, because what lies ahead is too much for him. Rest, food and company come first.

After losing his children, his wealth and his health, Job wishes he had never been born and asks why life is given to people in misery. He says it aloud, to God and to his friends. The book keeps his words, and it does not end in chapter 3; his anguish is the beginning of a longer road that leads him to meet God.

Paul tells a church that in Asia he was crushed beyond his strength, so that he despaired of life itself. He does not hide it to look strong. He says it taught him to rely on God who raises the dead, and he thanks the church whose prayers helped carry him through.

Psalm 88 is the one psalm that never turns from complaint to confidence. It ends with darkness as the man's closest companion. And yet it begins by calling God the God of my salvation, and he keeps crying out day and night. Faith here looks like not letting go, even when there is no feeling left.

David asks where he could go to get away from God, and every place he names, the heights, the depths, the far side of the sea, God is already there. Even darkness that seems to cover everything is not dark to God.

A psalm of thanks for rescue admits that the righteous have many troubles. What it promises is God's nearness to people whose hearts are broken and whose spirits are crushed. It does not say the brokenhearted are failing.

God introduces his chosen servant, whom the Gospels see fulfilled in Jesus (Matthew 12:18-21). He will not shout or crush. A reed that is already bent he will not snap, and a wick that is barely smoking he will not put out. He handles what is nearly broken with care.

The writer has described his affliction in the bleakest pictures in the book. Then he does something deliberate: he calls to mind what he knows of God's character. Hope begins not as a feeling but as a remembered truth, held on to one morning at a time.

Paul names everything that might come between a believer and God, trouble, hunger, danger, death and life, the present and the future, and says none of it can separate us from the love of God in Christ. The chapter that began with no condemnation ends with no separation.

whole: If you are thinking about ending your life, please do not stay alone with it. Tell someone today, a person you trust, a doctor, a pastor, or a crisis line where you live, and if you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn. Everything below can wait until you have done that.

Thoughts like these are more common than people say, even among people of deep faith. They often come with exhaustion, grief, shame, depression, long pain or a loss that has not been spoken about. They can feel like clear thinking: that the pain will never change, that you are a burden, that others would be better off. Those thoughts are real, and they are heavy. They are not the truth about you. Pain narrows what a person can see, and the narrowing is part of the pain.

The Bible does not pretend that faithful people never feel this. Elijah asked God to take his life. Job wished he had never been born. Paul despaired of life itself. Psalm 88 ends in darkness. What is striking is how God meets them. He does not lecture Elijah; he gives him sleep, bread and company, and only later speaks. He does not condemn Job's cry. He brought Paul through by people who prayed. The God of the Bible is not waiting for you to feel better before he comes near. He is near the brokenhearted now, and he handles a bruised reed without breaking it.

So the wisdom here is simple and urgent. Do the next small thing: tell one person, eat something, sleep, see a doctor, let someone sit with you. Seeing a doctor about this is wise and is not a lack of faith; what lies under these thoughts can often be treated. Let others carry what you cannot, as Paul let the church pray for him. If you can pray, pray honestly, even in the words of Psalm 88. And hold on to what you cannot feel right now: that nothing in all creation, not this darkness and not this night, can separate you from the love of God in Christ Jesus. Your life is not over, and it is not yours alone. Stay.
sit: Who is one person you could tell today, and what is the first sentence you would say to them?

prayer.lead: A prayer of David when his heart was faint. If you have no words of your own, these are enough.

careLines.text: But if darkness feels like your closest companion, please do not carry it alone.
Tell someone you trust today: a doctor, a pastor or a friend.
Sorrow that lasts, or that takes away sleep, hope or the wish to go on, is worth taking to a doctor, and doing so is not a lack of faith.
If you have thoughts of hurting yourself, speak to someone today: a doctor, a pastor, a trusted friend, or a crisis line in your country.
If you are in danger right now, call your local emergency number.
The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
